questions.q: According to the cost model defined in the lesson, what is the formula for the total cost to process a batch of size B?
questions.why: The lesson explicitly defines the total cost formula as Cost(B) = FIXED_OVERHEAD + (PER_ITEM_COST * B) in the 'Under the hood' section.

questions.q: In the lab results, what was the calculated throughput for a batch size of 16?
questions.why: The lab output line 'RESULT throughput_bs_16 = 6.10501' directly provides this value.

questions.q: Why does the lesson state that if you cannot batch efficiently on a single device, sharding across multiple devices will just multiply your inefficiency?
options: Sharding requires more memory than batching.
Sharding increases the fixed overhead per item.
Sharding relies on the same fundamental principle of amortization, so poor single-device efficiency scales up.
Sharding is only possible if the batch size is 1.
questions.answer: Sharding relies on the same fundamental principle of amortization, so poor single-device efficiency scales up.
questions.why: The 'Why this matters' section states: 'If you cannot batch efficiently on a single device, sharding across multiple devices will just multiply your inefficiency.' This implies that the core efficiency gain (amortization) must work on a single unit first.

questions.q: What is the primary risk associated with ignoring memory fragmentation in a scaled deployment, as described in the lesson?
options: A batch size that fits in theory might fail in practice due to fragmentation.
The GPU will automatically reduce the batch size to 1.
The fixed overhead will increase exponentially.
questions.answer: A batch size that fits in theory might fail in practice due to fragmentation.
questions.why: Under 'Common mistakes', point 2 states: 'A batch size that fits in theory might fail in practice due to fragmentation.'

questions.q: According to the lesson, what two specific states must a system distinguish between when cancelling a job to prevent VRAM leaks?
questions.why: The 'In ComfyUI' section states: 'Ensure your cancellation logic distinguishes between "running" and "pending" jobs.' It explains that running jobs need to be interrupted to free VRAM, while pending jobs can be dequeued.
